title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
The failure here is a claim of absence that was not true. Tesla told a grieving family that the fatal crash data from one of its cars was gone, and a hacker later showed that the cars retain that data. Reporting on the same case states that the data showed the vehicle detected a hazard before the fatal crash, which is the opposite of a record that does not exist.

The claim was made after the crash, in the evidence-gathering and litigation stage, not in the operation of the vehicle itself. Catching it required independent forensic access to the vehicle's stored logs rather than reliance on the manufacturer's account of what it kept. A jury ordered Tesla to pay more than $240 million, and a judge later upheld a $243 million verdict, with the reported figures differing between outlets.

What is not established from the material here is the substance of the reporting itself, because the summary supplied is a corrupted-document error message rather than a summary. The titles describe a jury verdict and a judge's ruling upholding it, and a verdict is not a finding of intent. The underlying facts of the crash are not established by these headlines.
